unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply two-identifier verification to confirm the correct patient before care, procedures, specimens, and disclosure of information.
- Protect patient privacy by applying safeguards and minimum-necessary practices to protected health information in the office.
- Explain the role and proper use of chaperones and describe how to preserve patient dignity during care.
- Recognize and escalate identity, privacy, dignity, and scope-of-practice concerns to the appropriate person.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Checking two identifiers is like making sure the lunchbox with your name on it is really yours before you take a bite.

### Question 2

Before you take something from someone, you check their full name and birthday, like checking a nametag and a secret code instead of just guessing by where they are sitting.

### Question 3

Using name plus birthday is like two locks on a diary: both must match before you open it.

### Question 4

A room number is like a parking spot number—it tells you where the car is, not whose car it is.

### Question 5

It is like double-checking you grabbed the right folder before a big meeting, so you do not hand your homework to the wrong person.

### Question 6

It is like asking someone to tell you their locker combination instead of you reading it and them just nodding yes.

### Question 7

It is like re-checking your ticket before boarding each connecting flight, not just once at the first gate.

### Question 8

If someone cannot tell you their name, you check their ID bracelet and their chart, like reading a lost dog's collar tag.

### Question 9

It is like checking the delivery person's ID and your order slip before handing over a package, not just because they know your address.

### Question 10

Two kids in class named Taylor need more than a first name—you check the last name and birthday, like telling twins apart.

### Question 11

The wristband is like a nametag you read before a race so you hand the right medal to the right runner.

### Question 12

The photo ID is like showing your library card—the librarian checks your name matches the account before checking out books.

### Question 13

If the name on a package does not match the one on your door, you do not just scribble a new name—you ask the post office to sort it out.

### Question 14

It is like calling a friend by the nickname they love while still using their full name on official school forms.

### Question 15

When a friend picks up your pizza, the shop still checks the order details—it does not just trust whoever says your name.

### Question 16

It is like making sure each puzzle piece has its own matching corner, so you do not glue two different pictures together.

### Question 17

It is like signing your name on a form to show you double-checked your work before handing it in.

### Question 18

It is like searching a locker room and matching both the number and the name tag before opening the locker.

### Question 19

It is like matching a baby animal to its mom by their matching tags at the shelter.

### Question 20

You show your ID before the front desk hands over anything with your name on it, every single time.

### Question 21

It is like a secret handshake that keeps a stranger from pretending to be you at the front desk.

### Question 22

It is like a seatbelt: you buckle it every trip, not just on long highway drives.

### Question 23

PHI is like a box of clues—name, birthday, and health details—that together point to one specific person.

### Question 24

You close the door when you change clothes at home—the same rule applies at the doctor's office.

### Question 25

Knocking is like asking 'May I come in?' instead of barging into a room.

### Question 26

You would not announce your friend's secret in a crowded elevator—you save it for a quiet room.

### Question 27

It is like whispering a secret instead of shouting it across the cafeteria.

### Question 28

It is like angling your phone away so the person next to you cannot read your text messages.

### Question 29

It is like locking your locker when you leave the gym instead of leaving it wide open.

### Question 30

It is like shredding an old bank statement instead of tossing it whole into the bin.

### Question 31

It is like only opening your front door when you have checked who is there and why.

### Question 32

It is like the school nurse sharing a health note with the PE teacher so you can sit out gym—no special form needed.

### Question 33

It is like being able to look at your own report card any time, but not your classmates'.

### Question 34

It is like telling the teacher your grade was entered wrong and asking to have it fixed.

### Question 35

It is like the rules sheet a game hands you before you play, telling you how your information will be used.

### Question 36

If you mailed a letter to the wrong house, you would tell an adult right away instead of hoping it comes back.

### Question 37

You always ask before taking someone's picture, and you use it only the way they agreed to.

### Question 38

It is like signing just your name on a list instead of writing your whole life story for the room to see.

### Question 39

It is like checking the address twice and sealing the envelope before mailing something private.

### Question 40

It is like sending a secret through a locked mailbox instead of writing it on a public bulletin board.

### Question 41

It is like only telling your secret to the friend your parents said could know.

### Question 42

It is like deciding for yourself whether to bring a friend into the room when you talk to a counselor.

### Question 43

It is like not telling one friend another friend's private business, no matter how nicely they ask.

### Question 44

It is like peeking in someone's locker just because you are curious—even if you tell no one, it is still wrong.

### Question 45

It is like keeping your class list in a folder instead of taping it to the classroom door.

### Question 46

It is like erasing the name and address off a picture so no one knows whose it is.

### Question 47

It is like a name being briefly overheard at a ticket counter even though the clerk is being careful.

### Question 48

It is like keeping your diary in a locked drawer instead of on the kitchen table.

### Question 49

When you are not sure if you are allowed to share something, you ask a grown-up instead of guessing.

### Question 50

It is like giving the repair shop only the part they need to fix your car, not the whole owner's manual.

### Question 51

A chaperone is like a trusted helper who stays in the room so everyone feels safe and nothing unfair happens.

### Question 52

A chaperone is like a buddy who sits with you so you are not alone and everything stays fair.

### Question 53

It is like asking if you want a friend to stay with you during a scary part of a movie.

### Question 54

It is like letting a student choose to talk to a teacher they feel more comfortable with.

### Question 55

It is like writing in a log who was in the room, so there is a clear record later.

### Question 56

A chaperone stands like a quiet helper nearby, close enough to see but not hovering.

### Question 57

It is like respecting when a friend says 'I'm okay on my own, thanks.'

### Question 58

A chaperone is like having an extra helper for the parts of care that feel most personal.

### Question 59

A chaperone is like a teammate who stays with you so you feel braver.

### Question 60

A chaperone is like a helper who holds the flashlight, not the one who reads the x-ray.

### Question 61

The assistant is like a helpful referee on the field, not the coach calling the plays.

### Question 62

A chaperone is like a referee who makes the game fair for both teams.

### Question 63

It is like the right to have a trusted adult in the room when you talk to someone important.

### Question 64

For kids, the rules are like a field trip: an adult stays close to keep everyone safe.

### Question 65

A chaperone is like a buddy who stays with you; an interpreter is like a translator who helps two people understand each other.

### Question 66

It is like everyone on a team learning the same playbook so the game runs smoothly.

### Question 67

If something feels wrong, you tell a trusted grown-up instead of keeping it a secret.

### Question 68

Having a buddy in the room does not mean you stop using a towel to stay covered.

### Question 69

Treating someone with dignity is like treating them as an important guest, not just a name on a list.

### Question 70

It is like closing the curtain when you change at the pool so no one sees.

### Question 71

You call people by the name they like, not a silly name you invented.

### Question 72

You would want someone to tell you before they move your chair, not just yank it.

### Question 73

It is like opening your jacket just enough to show the doctor the sore spot, not taking the whole jacket off.

### Question 74

It is like waiting outside until your friend says they are dressed again.

### Question 75

It is like making room for a friend's family tradition even if it is different from yours.

### Question 76

You help a friend in a wheelchair get comfortable and talk to them, not about them.

### Question 77

You can help someone without having to agree with everything about them.

### Question 78

Treating people with respect makes them feel safe, like a coach who believes in every player.

### Question 79

If a friend tells you something felt wrong, you listen and tell an adult who can help.

### Question 80

It is like telling your teacher first when something is wrong, not posting it online.

### Question 81

When you are not sure if a job is yours, you ask the person in charge first.

### Question 82

If you write in the wrong notebook, you tell the teacher right away so it can be fixed.

### Question 83

When you are unsure, ask for help—that is the bravest and safest choice.
